title: Hereditary discrepancy and factorization norms (AimPL) — Problem 1.8: Reverse Banaszczyk-type problems

problems.sourceStatement: Say that a convex body $K$ has property B if for any set of vectors of length no more than $c$ (some small constant), there exists a signing of them s.t. this signed sum lies inside $K$. What is the convex body with the smallest gaussian volume which has property $B$?
problems.problem: Characterize the convex body of minimum Gaussian volume that has 'property B': for every finite set of vectors of length at most some small constant $c$, there exist signs such that the signed sum lies in $K$.
problems.wordDescription: This is the reverse (extremal) direction of Banaszczyk's vector-balancing theorem, which states that every convex body $K$ of Gaussian measure at least $1/2$ has property B for vectors of length at most $1/5$ (up to a constant factor). The question asks for the smallest Gaussian volume a body with property B can have — i.e., how tight the $1/2$ threshold really is. The threshold is known to be 'essentially tight' in a weak sense (a body of Gaussian measure $< 1/2$ can fail to contain 0, and the halfspace argument shows $\gamma(K) \geq 1/2$ forces $0 \in K$), but the extremal question about the true minimum Gaussian volume among property-B bodies is open. Daniel Dadush's remark recorded on the AimPL page shows that property B forces $\mathbb{E}\|G\|_K = (\log n)^{O(1)}$ for a standard Gaussian $G$, i.e. the Gaussian measure of $K$ is at least $\exp(-(\log n)^{O(1)})$ — so the answer lies between $\approx 1/2$ and $\exp(-\mathrm{polylog}\, n)$.
problems.mathematicalConditions: Setting. Let $K \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a symmetric convex body and $\gamma_n$ the standard Gaussian measure. Banaszczyk's theorem: if $\gamma_n(K) \geq 1/2$ then for any number $m$ of vectors $v_1, \dots, v_m \in B_2^n$ there are signs with $\sum_i \epsilon_i v_i \in 5K$. Say $K$ has property $B$ (the 'Banaszczyk property') if there is a constant $C$ such that for every finite family $v_1, \dots, v_m \in B_2^n$ there are signs $\epsilon$ with $\sum_i \epsilon_i v_i \in C K$; write $\mathrm{vb}(B_2^n, K)$ for the least such $C$ (the vector-balancing constant of $(B_2^n, K)$). Problem (reverse Banaszczyk). Characterize the bodies with property $B$: is it true that $\mathrm{vb}(B_2^n, K) = O(1)$ implies $\gamma_n(cK) \geq 1/2$ for some absolute constant $c$ (equivalently, that $\mathbb{E}\|G\|_K = O(1)$ for a standard Gaussian $G$)? More generally, determine $\mathrm{vb}(B_2^n, K)$ in terms of Gaussian (or other geometric) parameters of $K$ up to constant factors. Benchmarks. Upper bound: $\mathrm{vb}(B_2^n, K) \leq 5t$ whenever $\gamma_n(tK) \geq 1/2$ (Banaszczyk 1998), so $\mathrm{vb}(B_2^n, K) = O(\mathbb{E}\|G\|_K)$. Lower bound (volume argument, cf. Problem 1.5): $\mathrm{vb}(B_2^n, K) \geq c\,(\mathrm{vol}(B_2^n)/\mathrm{vol}(K))^{1/n}$. The Komlós conjecture is exactly the statement that $K = B_\infty^n$ (for which $\mathbb{E}\|G\|_K = \Theta(\sqrt{\log n})$) has property $B$, so a full reverse Banaszczyk theorem would refute Komlós. Workshop result (Dadush, recorded as a comment): if $K$ has property $B$ then $\mathbb{E}\|G\|_K = (\log n)^{O(1)}$; i.e. property $B$ implies $\gamma_n((\log n)^{O(1)} K) \geq 1/2$. Dadush-Garg-Lovett-Nikolov (2019) discuss the tightness of the Gaussian-measure threshold $1/2$ in Banaszczyk's theorem. Complete resolution. Either (A) a proof that property $B$ implies $\mathbb{E}\|G\|_K = O(1)$ (which would disprove the Komlós conjecture, since $\mathbb{E}\|G\|_{B_\infty^n} = \Theta(\sqrt{\log n})$), or (B) a body $K$ with property $B$ and $\mathbb{E}\|G\|_K \to \infty$ (the Komlós conjecture, if true, provides $K = B_\infty^n$), together with a characterization of $\mathrm{vb}(B_2^n, K)$ up to constants by a geometric parameter. Minimal progress that counts as a solution of this record. Any of: (i) improving the workshop bound $\mathbb{E}\|G\|_K = (\log n)^{O(1)}$ for bodies with property $B$ to $\mathbb{E}\|G\|_K = O(\sqrt{\log n})$ (which would be tight if the Komlós conjecture holds), or to any explicit exponent smaller than the one provable by the workshop argument; (ii) a body $K$ with $\mathrm{vb}(B_2^n, K) = O(1)$ and $\mathbb{E}\|G\|_K = \omega(1)$ (unconditionally); (iii) a characterization of $\mathrm{vb}(B_2^n, K)$ up to $\mathrm{polylog}(n)$ factors for all symmetric convex $K$ (e.g. in terms of $\mathbb{E}\|G\|_K$ and volumes of sections), or up to constants for all unconditional $K$; (iv) a polynomial-time algorithm that, given a membership oracle for $K$ and $v_1, \dots, v_m \in B_2^n$, finds signs with $\sum \epsilon_i v_i \in O(\mathrm{vb}(B_2^n, K)\cdot\mathrm{polylog}(n))\, K$.

comments.body: During the workshop it was shown that if $K$ has property $B$, then $\mathbb{E} \|G\|_K = (\log n)^{O(1)}$, where $G$ is a standard Gaussian random vector.

literature.title: W. Banaszczyk, Balancing vectors and Gaussian measures of n-dimensional convex bodies, Random Structures & Algorithms 12(4):351-360, 1998
literature.description: Proves the vector-balancing theorem for convex bodies of Gaussian measure at least $1/2$; applied to a scaled $\ell_\infty$ ball it gives $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ for the Komlós problem and $O(\sqrt{k \log n})$ for degree-$k$ set systems.

literature.title: D. Dadush, S. Garg, S. Lovett, A. Nikolov, Towards a constructive version of Banaszczyk's vector balancing theorem, APPROX/RANDOM 2016; Theory of Computing 15(15):1-58, 2019
literature.description: Algorithmic version of Banaszczyk's theorem; also discusses the tightness of the Gaussian-measure threshold $1/2$ and the relation between property-$B$-type statements and Gaussian measure.

literature.title: N. Bansal, D. Dadush, S. Garg, S. Lovett, The Gram-Schmidt walk: a cure for the Banaszczyk blues, STOC 2018; Theory of Computing 15(21):1-27, 2019
literature.description: Constructive version of Banaszczyk's full vector-balancing theorem (for arbitrary convex bodies of Gaussian measure at least $1/2$), via the Gram-Schmidt walk.
